one_liner: Meta's work-stealing C++ thread pool and parallel-algorithms library, faster than oneTBB on small/medium parallel-for loops.
what_it_does: Dispenso is a compute-bound parallelism library: a work-stealing ThreadPool plus parallel_for, parallel_invoke, for_each, TaskSet/ConcurrentTaskSet, task graphs, pipelines, thread-safe shared Futures, and concurrent containers (ConcurrentVector, ring buffers, RWLock). It targets the same space as oneTBB and OpenMP, not std::async: you construct explicit ThreadPool/TaskSet objects and wrap loops with dispenso::parallel_for rather than calling a single free function. It is used in hundreds of internal projects at Meta.
how_it_is_fast: A work-stealing ThreadPool underlies all scheduling; parallel_for supports static (equal up-front chunking, lowest overhead) or adaptive (stripe-based work-stealing that prefers same-L3-cache victims) chunking, tuned via minItemsPerChunk. Cascading parallel_for lets independent loops share the pool without oversubscription, which the project reports as a 32-50% win over TBB in production after porting. Lock-free primitives (a ChaseLevDeque work-stealing deque, MPMC/SPSC ring buffers, a bundled moodycamel::ConcurrentQueue) back the scheduler and containers with low per-task overhead.
when_to_use: Nested or many independent parallel_for calls that would oversubscribe threads under TBB/OpenMP
Need thread-safe shared futures with then()/when_all()/when_any(), which TBB lacks
Need ASAN/TSAN-clean concurrent C++ (TBB is not sanitizer-friendly)
Small-to-medium parallel-for workloads at low-to-mid thread counts, where the project's own EPYC-Genoa benchmark shows 1.5-3.5x over tbb::parallel_for
Codebase pinned to a C++14 baseline that still wants a modern TBB/OpenMP alternative
when_not_to_use: Very high thread counts on large cores: on the project's own 166-core EPYC data, TBB is faster at 128 and 166 threads for the 1M-element case, and at 1-4 and 32 threads for the 100M-element case
I/O-bound workloads — the FAQ explicitly says pool threads that block on I/O waste scheduling capacity and points to Folly instead
Need OpenMP-style '#pragma omp reduction' syntax — dispenso has no first-class reduction API, only manual per-thread accumulation
Need GPU/CUDA task graphs — TaskFlow supports CUDA graph mapping, dispenso does not
macOS builds needing explicit CPU-pinning — CpuSet::bindCurrentThread() is a documented no-op there

integration.dependencies: moodycamel::concurrentqueue (bundled by default under dispenso/third-party, or an installed copy via -DDISPENSO_USE_SYSTEM_CONCURRENTQUEUE=ON)
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (default, fully supported); C++17/C++20 swap in std facilities and add concept constraints but change no behavior; CMake 3.12+
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64/ARM64, macOS x86-64/ARM64, Windows x86-64/ARM64, FreeBSD (full); Android ARM64 (partial CPU-affinity/topology)
integration.thread_safety: ThreadPool and ConcurrentTaskSet support scheduling from multiple threads simultaneously; ConcurrentVector supports concurrent push_back with iterators/references that stay valid across growth, but 'not all operations are concurrent-safe' per the docs. Library is built and tested clean under ASAN/TSAN.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false — explicit ThreadPool/TaskSet objects and its own parallel_for/Future API, not TBB's implicit global arena or std::async's per-call thread; the project ships separate TBB and OpenMP migration guides rather than calling itself a drop-in

gotchas: Exceptions thrown inside parallel_for/TaskSet lambdas are captured, not propagated immediately; the first one rethrows only when wait() runs (or the TaskSet destructor), and other in-flight tasks keep running
Builds with -fno-exceptions call abort() instead of throwing

moodycamel::ConcurrentQueue is a by-value member of ThreadPool, so it's part of dispenso's ABI — building the library against one concurrentqueue version while a consumer compiles against another is an undiagnosed ODR violation
DISPENSO_SHARED_LIB defaults to ON, so a static build has to be requested explicitly
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Versus other oneTBB-beating siblings here (TooManyCooks, libfork, Taskflow — all coroutine/C++20-leaning with bigger peak ratios in their own benchmarks), pick dispenso when you need a C++14-compatible, sanitizer-clean, explicitly-controlled thread pool rather than a coroutine scheduler, or when your workload is many independent/nested parallel_for loops where dispenso's cascading scheduling avoids oversubscription. Versus the std::thread/std::async-only siblings (Boost.Fiber, utl::parallel, BS::thread_pool, meet1214/thread-pool), dispenso is the pick when your actual incumbent is TBB or OpenMP rather than bare std primitives.
verified_claims_summary: On Meta's public benchmark dashboard (GNU 11.5.0, C++20, CMake Release build, AMD EPYC-Genoa host: 166 cores, 224GB RAM, Linux 6.16.1, TBB 2023.1.0), the summing_for microbenchmark shows dispenso::parallel_for beating tbb::parallel_for at low-to-mid thread counts: 1.61x at 1M elements/1 thread (279us vs 450us), 3.48x at 1M elements/8 threads (50.6us vs 175.8us), and 1.53x at 100M elements/16 threads (2.27ms vs 3.47ms). I independently pulled results/linux_x64.json from the repo and confirmed its machine_info block (compiler, standard, build type, CPU, core count) matches the record exactly. The same sweep also has TBB ahead at 128+ threads and at several low-thread 100M-element points, so the claimed numbers are favorable picks from a mixed comparison, not a uniform win.
status_note: Actively maintained by Meta (last commit 2026-09-02, current release v1.6.2, packaged for Conan/vcpkg/Homebrew/conda-forge/Fedora); MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but it is a built static/shared CMake library rather than header-only, with one bundled MIT/BSD-compatible dependency (moodycamel::concurrentqueue).
